extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, and literate readers (writers of satire and moral essays)
extracted.subtask_short: writing moral satire and character sketches
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing satirical essays, theatrical character-drawing, and moral fables that influence audiences by honest characterization, allegory, and careful observation. Emphasizes techniques for moral reproof, comedic targeting, and stylistic restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty in Characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Poets will attempt it with the Honesty which becomes their Characters.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present characters truthfully and consistently with their moral makeup; honesty of depiction allows characters to move readers' hearts and serve as instruments of reproof or instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single Darling Vice per Character
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘There is seldom a Person devoted to above one Darling Vice at a time…’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus each character around one predominant failing (vice) rather than piling on multiple vices; this makes the character recognizably human and provides a clear target for satire or moral correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine Virtue with Wit and Amiable Qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘A Man that is Temperate, Generous, Valiant, Chaste, Faithful and Honest, may, at the same time, have Wit, Humour, Mirth, Good-breeding, and Gallantry.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict virtuous characters as lively and entertaining as well as morally sound; show occasions that reveal their virtues so they can correct and move readers who are given up to pleasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for Wholesome Influence; Avoid Spurious Oaths
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Steele's Plays… absolutely discarding the customary way of enforcing feeble dialogues by the spurious force of oaths, and aiming at a wholesome influence upon his audience.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid cheap shocks, vulgar oaths, or other rhetorical tricks that substitute for real characterization or argument; favour language and situations that have a beneficial, morally improving effect on the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrain Excessive Passion and Climax
rubrics_metrics.description: Footnote example: a passionate climax in a play was 'retracted' or 'retrench[ed]' in later editions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise moderation in scenes of intense passion; excessive or overwrought climaxes may be trimmed in later revisions to preserve decorum and the intended moral effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct Laughter at Follies, Not Mere Humiliation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reader laughed ‘at the Idiot, the German Courtier, the Gaper, the Merry-Andrew, the Haberdasher, the Biter, the Butt…’ (Spectator's defence of what was laughed at).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim comedic ridicule at follies, foibles, and social types rather than gratuitously humiliating individuals; make clear targets (stereotypes of folly) so the humour instructs rather than merely insults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Observational Detail as Material for Satire
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘I have with great Pains and Industry made my Observations from time to time upon these Sages; and having now all Materials ready, am compiling a Treatise, wherein I shall set forth the Rise and Progress… their Maxims, Austerities, Manner of living, &c.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect concrete, lived details (maxims, routines, mannerisms, exercises, places frequented) through patient observation; these particulars ground satire and give authority and texture to caricature or mock-historical accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compile Maxims, Examples, and Manner-of-Living
rubrics_metrics.description: The correspondent promises to set forth ‘their Maxims, Austerities, Manner of living…’ as the basis of a treatise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When exposing or parodying a group, include explicit maxims and typical behaviors as representative evidence; provide sketches, anecdotes, and exempla to illustrate the satire's claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ Allegory and Personification for Moral Lessons
rubrics_metrics.description: A fable-like account: two Tyrants called Luxury and Avarice, with officers (Pleasure, Mirth, Pomp, Fashion) and counsellors (Plenty, Poverty) contending for hearts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personify abstract vices or virtues and use dialogue/fable structure to make moral and political points vivid and memorable; such allegory permits generalization and theatrical presentation of competing principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Classical Allusion and Translation to Lend Authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent use of Latin quotations (Virgil, Horace, Persius, etc.) and reference to Dryden's translation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate classical citations and translations to bolster intellectual authority and to create parallels between ancient examples and contemporary conduct; compare original phrasing and translation when instructive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply Historical Analogy to Contemporary Morals
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘When a Government flourishes in Conquests… it naturally falls into all the Pleasures of Luxury…’ (drawing on Latin historian Sallust and Roman example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical precedent and analogy (e.g., Roman decline into luxury and avarice) to illuminate present social or political tendencies; analogies should be explicit and used to generalize moral lessons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Epistolary and Dialogic Forms to Engage Readers
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper includes letters from correspondents and replies (e.g., humorous exchanges about laughter, deformity, and visits to Oxford).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt letters, imagined court replies, and mock-royal dispatches as devices to present multiple voices, test arguments, incite reader response, and stage satirical positions without didactic directness.
